# Agent instructions for this repository

This repository is the home of a container image that runs
[OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) for Python development, tuned for optimization
work with Google OR-Tools. GitHub Actions builds and publishes the image to GHCR
for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64` on every push to `main`, on a schedule, and
on demand. Read [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md) for the layout and
the pipeline, and [docs/updating.md](docs/updating.md) for versioning.

## Environment limits

- Docker and Podman are not available in the default working environment. The
  image is built only by the GitHub Actions workflow, so validate changes
  statically and let CI build them.
- The base is Debian (`python:<version>-slim`), not Alpine. Python wheels are
  `manylinux`, and OR-Tools is the reason: it publishes no musllinux wheel and
  no source distribution.
- Run the static checks below after touching the corresponding file types; they
  must pass before committing.

| File types                         | Check                                                                       |
| ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `*.sh`                             | `shellcheck` and `shfmt -i 2 -d` (must print no diff)                       |
| `*.md`                             | `prettier --check --prose-wrap preserve --embedded-language-formatting off` |
| `*.yml`, `*.yaml` (workflows, k8s) | `yq -e . file`                                                              |
| `*.json`, `*.jsonc`                | `jq -e .` (strip `//` comment lines from `jsonc` first)                     |
| `*.py`                             | `python3 -m py_compile file`                                                |

Format changed Markdown with
`prettier --write --prose-wrap preserve --embedded-language-formatting off`
before committing; it pads tables so they stay aligned in a terminal.

## Rules

- **Versions are never hardcoded** in the `Containerfile` or the workflow.
  `scripts/resolve-versions.sh` resolves OpenCode, OR-Tools, the newest CPython
  that OR-Tools supports, and yq at CI time; `versions.json` is the pinned
  record and is updated only by the `update-pins` bot PR.
- **OR-Tools bounds Python.** The CPython minor is derived from the `cp3XY`
  wheels of the newest `ortools` release. Never bump Python past what OR-Tools
  ships wheels for: there is no sdist to fall back to.
- **Secrets are host-side only.** Never commit a `.env` file, never print or
  echo tokens. `.env.example` is the template; it is baked into the image at
  `/home/opencode/.env.example` for the `env-setup` agent skill.
- **Documentation:** English, in `docs/` as short single-topic pages; link every
  page from the README index and cross-link related pages. Keep `README.md` at
  100 lines or fewer. Update the affected docs in the same change as behavior,
  configuration, or setup.
- **Commits:** English, Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`,
  `chore:`, ...). Commit after each logical change, not one giant commit.
- **Two AGENTS.md files are different things.** The root file is for agents
  working on this repository. `config/opencode/AGENTS.md` is baked into the
  image and instructs the agent that runs inside it, for Python work. Do not mix
  their concerns.

## After pushing

The push to `main` triggers the `Build` workflow. Watch the run (GitHub Actions
or `gh run list` / `gh run watch`), and on failure read the logs
(`gh run view <id> --log`) before changing anything. The smoke test runs per
architecture: it checks the image default, starts the server and answers
`GET /api/info` with Basic auth, and installs OR-Tools in a throwaway venv to
solve a small CP-SAT model.

The workflow also maintains the `status` branch: a single commit holding
`status.json`, the data behind the README's last-build badge. It is written by
CI only; never edit or merge that branch.

# Instructions

## Language rules

- **Conversation with the user:** in the language the user writes in.
- **Code:** identifiers, variables, functions, classes, file names — in English.
- **Code comments:** in English.
- **Git commit messages:** in English, Conventional Commits format (feat:, fix:, docs:, etc.).
- **Documentation, log messages, error messages, CLI output:** in English.

## Style

- Keep code idiomatic and clean.
- Keep changes consistent with the structure, naming and patterns of the
  surrounding code.

## Tooling

The image ships a Python development toolchain. Prefer these tools over ad-hoc
alternatives.

- Environments and packages: `uv`. Use `uv venv`, `uv add`, `uv sync`,
  `uv pip`, `uvx` and `uv run`. Never install packages into the system
  interpreter with `pip`; if a script needs an environment, create one with
  `uv`.
- Python versions: `uv python install 3.12` (or another version) and a
  `.python-version` file in the project. The interpreter baked into the image is
  the newest CPython that OR-Tools publishes wheels for; do not raise the
  project's Python requirement beyond it.
- Lint and format: `ruff check`, `ruff format`. Types: `mypy`. Tests: `pytest`.
- Hooks: `pre-commit`.
- Profiling: `py-spy` (`py-spy top`, `py-spy record -o profile.svg -- python
model.py`), including native OR-Tools calls.
- Search: `rg` (ripgrep), `fd`, `ast-grep` (also available as `sg`) for
  structural search and rewriting.
- JSON/YAML: `jq`, `yq`.
- Forge: `gh` for GitHub, `glab` for GitLab (issues, MRs, pipelines,
  releases); Forgejo through the REST API.
- Shell scripts: `shellcheck`, `shfmt`.
- Native builds: `gcc`/`g++`, `make`, `pkg-config` and the development headers
  (`libssl-dev`, `libffi-dev`, `zlib1g-dev`, `libsqlite3-dev`) are available for
  C extensions.
- Markdown: the repository CI checks formatting with `prettier`, which is not
  installed here (it needs Node). Keep tables aligned by hand and do not
  reformat whole files.

## OR-Tools

- OR-Tools is a project dependency, not part of the image: add it with
  `uv add ortools` and pin the version in the project. Wheels exist for glibc
  only, which is why the image is Debian-based.
- OR-Tools pins `protobuf<6.34`; do not force a newer protobuf alongside it.
- CP-SAT is CPU- and memory-hungry: give the container enough resources
  (`--cpus`, `--memory`) and tune `num_search_workers` in the solver
  parameters.
- HiGHS (`uv add highspy`), PuLP and Pyomo are project dependencies too; only
  open-source solvers are supported out of the box (CP-SAT, GLOP, SCIP,
  HiGHS).

## Git and forges

- Commits use `GIT_AUTHOR_*` and `GIT_COMMITTER_*` when they are set. Do not
  change the git identity in the repository or in the global config.
- GitHub: git over HTTPS uses the `gh` credential helper, which the entrypoint
  configures from `GH_TOKEN`. Use `gh` for issues, pull requests and releases;
  it reads `GH_TOKEN` from the environment.
- GitLab (optional): when `GITLAB_TOKEN` is set, git over HTTPS to the GitLab
  host (`GITLAB_URL`, default `https://gitlab.com`) is preconfigured by the
  entrypoint. Use `glab` for issues, MRs, pipelines and releases (it reads
  `GITLAB_TOKEN`; pass `--hostname` for self-hosted instances) or the REST API
  with the `PRIVATE-TOKEN` header.
- Forgejo (optional): when `FORGEJO_TOKEN` and `FORGEJO_URL` are set, git over
  HTTPS/HTTP to that instance is preconfigured by the entrypoint. Use the REST
  API (`<FORGEJO_URL>/api/v1/...`) with the `Authorization: token` header.
- Never print, log or commit `GH_TOKEN`, `GITLAB_TOKEN`, `FORGEJO_TOKEN` or
  other credentials.

## Container updates

OpenCode is baked into the image; it cannot update itself inside the
container. Never run `opencode upgrade` or edit the installed binary. Updates
are published by the GitHub Actions workflow, so ask the user to pull a newer
image when a newer OpenCode is needed.

## Models

No model is pinned in the baked config. Until the user connects a provider,
OpenCode serves its free built-in models (provider `opencode`) with no account
or key, and the session starts on one of them.

When the session runs on a free built-in model, mention it once at the start of
the conversation (in the user's language, one or two sentences): the session
runs on a free model that ships with OpenCode, and for other models the user can
connect a provider with the TUI's `/connect` command and then pick a model in
the model picker. The TUI's sidebar already shows the `/connect` hint, so keep
the mention brief.

If the user asks about an environment file instead, offer to create a `.env`
file in the project folder yourself: copy the template
`/home/opencode/.env.example` to `.env` in the working directory (the project is
mounted, so the file lands on the host), and tell the user to fill in
`OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and add `--env-file .env` to the run command (the optional
launcher finds the file on its own).

Offer it once; do not repeat it unless the user asks, and do not push it if the
user is content with the built-in model.

## Secrets

Secrets (provider API keys, the server password, forge tokens, a private
package index URL) are passed at runtime through the environment, or stored
once by the user with `opencode auth login` or the TUI's `/connect` command (a
stored account wins over the matching environment variable, for example over
`OPENROUTER_API_KEY`). The runtime env template is baked into the image at
`/home/opencode/.env.example`. When a required variable is missing or empty,
use the `env-setup` skill to offer the user a copy of the template. Never write
secrets into the repository, print them in output, commit a `.env` file, or run
`opencode auth export`.

## sudo

Passwordless sudo is available inside this container. Use it only to install
software that is missing for the current task.

Allowed:

- `sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends
<package>` after checking the package name with `apt-cache policy <package>`.
- Temporary build dependencies, removed in the same session.

Not allowed:

- Editing, creating, moving or deleting project files through sudo. Container
  root maps to a subuid on the host and would break project file ownership.
  All project changes go through the normal user.
- Running the agent, git, or language tooling as root.
- `apt-get upgrade`, removing base packages, or replacing system runtimes
  (system Python, uv).
- Installing Python packages with sudo: use `uv`, `uvx` or a project virtual
  environment instead.
- Changing `/etc/sudoers*`, `/etc/passwd`, or SSH/GPG configuration.

Rules:

- State the package and the reason before installing, and keep it minimal.
- Runtime installs live in the writable layer and disappear when the container
  exits. If a tool is needed permanently, tell the user so it can be added to
  the Containerfile.
- After installing, verify with `command -v <tool>` and the tool's version.
- Never use sudo to work around a permission error inside the project; fix the
  cause or ask the user.

# Env setup

Use this skill when a required runtime environment variable is missing or
empty, or when a model, provider or package index request fails with an
authentication error (for example HTTP 401, "missing API key", or a private
index rejecting anonymous access).

The image ships a documented runtime env template at
`/home/opencode/.env.example`. Values are passed at runtime only (`--env-file`
or a Kubernetes Secret) and are never baked into the image.

No key is required for the free built-in models: until the user connects a
provider, the session runs on OpenCode's free models (provider `opencode`).
The OpenRouter key is only needed for OpenRouter models; it arrives either in
the environment (`OPENROUTER_API_KEY`) or as a stored account from the TUI's
`/connect` command or `opencode auth login openrouter`. If the user wants
OpenRouter models and the key is missing or invalid, copying the template does
not fix it: tell the user to connect in the TUI with `/connect` (the key is
stored on the state volume) or to set `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` in the env file and
restart. Use this skill for the remaining variables.

## Check

List which variables are currently set:

```sh
env | grep -E '^(OPENROUTER_API_KEY|OPENCODE_PASSWORD|GH_TOKEN|GITLAB_TOKEN|FORGEJO_TOKEN|UV_INDEX_URL)=' || true
```

## Actions

1. List the missing variables in a table with their purpose. The template at
   `/home/opencode/.env.example` documents every variable.
2. Offer to copy the template into the working folder (the project directory is
   mounted from the host, so the file ends up on the host):

   ```sh
   cp /home/opencode/.env.example .env
   ```

3. Explain that the user fills in the values on the host and restarts the
   container with the file:

   - Docker/Podman: add `--env-file .env` to the run command and start the
     container again.
   - Kubernetes: update the `Secret` referenced by the Deployment and let the
     pod restart.

4. Remind the user:

   - Add `.env` to `.gitignore`; never commit the file.
   - Keep it readable only by the user: `chmod 600 .env`.
   - Never print or echo the values, and never write them into the repository
     or the logs.

## Variables

| Variable                                     | Purpose                                                                                                                                  |
| -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`                         | API key for OpenRouter models. Optional: the free built-in models work without it; the stored account wins over this variable.           |
| `OPENCODE_PASSWORD`                          | Password for the OpenCode server (HTTP API). Optional: when empty, the server generates one and prints it to the container log on start. |
| `GH_TOKEN`                                   | GitHub token for git over HTTPS and the `gh` CLI. Optional.                                                                              |
| `GITLAB_TOKEN`                               | GitLab token for git over HTTPS, the `glab` CLI and API calls. Optional.                                                                 |
| `GITLAB_URL`                                 | Self-hosted GitLab host (default `https://gitlab.com`). Optional.                                                                        |
| `FORGEJO_URL`                                | Forgejo/Gitea instance URL; required for `FORGEJO_TOKEN`. Optional.                                                                      |
| `FORGEJO_TOKEN`                              | Forgejo/Gitea token for git and the REST API. Optional.                                                                                  |
| `UV_INDEX_URL`                               | Private package index for `uv` (may contain a token in the URL). Optional.                                                               |
| `GIT_AUTHOR_NAME` / `GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL`       | Author identity for git commits. Optional.                                                                                               |
| `GIT_COMMITTER_NAME` / `GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL` | Committer identity for git commits. Optional.                                                                                            |

# opencode-python

[![Build](https://github.com/app/opencode-python/actions/workflows/build.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/app/opencode-python/actions/workflows/build.yml)
[![Last build](https://img.shields.io/endpoint?url=https%3A%2F%2Fraw.githubusercontent.com%2Fapp%2Fopencode-python%2Fstatus%2Fstatus.json)](https://github.com/app/opencode-python/actions/workflows/build.yml)

_A cozy little house for your coding agent: the venv is ready, Python is warm,
and OR-Tools has already optimized who sits by the fire._

A container image that runs [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) for Python
development, tuned for optimization work with Google OR-Tools. Nothing to
install: one run command from your project directory and the agent is working —
the TUI opens inside the container.

## Quick start

From the project directory you want the agent to work in:

Podman:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 \
  --name "opencode-$$" \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-python-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest
```

Docker (the same, with `--user` instead of `--userns`):

```bash
docker run -it --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  --name "opencode-$$" \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-python-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest
```

To pass secrets, add `--env-file` with a file of `NAME=value` lines (or
`-e NAME=value` for one). Most common variables (the full list:
[Passing secrets](docs/usage.md#passing-secrets)):

| Variable             | Purpose                               |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | API key for OpenRouter models         |
| `GH_TOKEN`           | GitHub token for git and the `gh` CLI |
| `OPENCODE_PASSWORD`  | server password (server mode only)    |

The image is published for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`, so Apple Silicon
runs it natively. State (sessions, connected accounts, extra Python versions)
is kept in the per-user volume `opencode-python-state-<user>`. The TUI opens on
OpenCode's free built-in model — start typing, no key needed. For other models,
connect OpenRouter with the TUI's `/connect` command. See
[Installation](docs/installation.md).

## The image

- **Rolling latest.** GitHub Actions builds and publishes the image to GHCR on
  every push and on a daily schedule (06:17 UTC), with the current upstream
  OpenCode, the newest CPython that OR-Tools supports, and the current yq. The
  schedule also compares the resolved versions with `versions.json` and opens a
  pull request when they differ — see [Updating](docs/updating.md).
- **Python toolchain.** CPython on Debian, `uv` for environments and tools,
  `ruff`, `basedpyright`, `mypy`, `pytest`, `pre-commit`, `py-spy`,
  `ast-grep`, plus git, `gh`, `glab` and the usual agent tooling — see
  [Toolchain](docs/toolchain.md).
- **Optimization ready.** glibc base with native OR-Tools wheels for both
  architectures, CI-verified — see [Optimization](docs/optimization.md).
- **Non-root.** The agent never runs as root: on Podman it is the image's
  uid 1000 mapped onto your host user, on Docker your host UID, with a
  restricted sudo policy.

## Three kinds of users

- A human in the TUI — the image default, as in the quick start above.
- A human in the web UI — server mode plus the pairing flow.
- An external agent — server mode plus the HTTP API (Basic auth, username
  `opencode`).

Server mode is an explicit command
(`opencode serve --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 4096`); see
[Usage](docs/usage.md) and [Access](docs/api.md). Running OpenCode in
Kubernetes: [Kubernetes](docs/kubernetes.md).

| [Usage](docs/usage.md)                     | Running the container, mounts, resources, secrets, commands     |
| [Access](docs/api.md)                      | TUI, web UI and the HTTP API for agents, Basic auth, OpenAPI    |

# Access

How the three kinds of users reach the agent. OpenCode lives only inside the
container; nothing is installed on the host.

## TUI

The image default. From the project directory:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 \
  --name "opencode-$$" \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-python-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest
```

See [Usage](usage.md#open-the-tui-default) for the mount layout (Docker: the
same with `--user` instead of `--userns`). The TUI talks to the local process
inside the container and needs no password.

## Web UI

The web UI is served by the
[server mode](usage.md#start-the-server-web-ui-http-api). To sign in, create a
pairing link from inside the running container:
`podman exec -it --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" <name> opencode pair`
(`<name>` is the container name, see [Logs](usage.md#logs)).

Open the printed link in a browser (the port must be published,
`-p 4096:4096`). Links work once and expire in 5 minutes; sessions last
30 days. Changing the server password signs every session out. Over SSH,
forward the server port and open the link locally.

## Authentication

Server mode is password-protected. Set `OPENCODE_PASSWORD` in the env file to
use a fixed password; when it is empty, the server generates a random one and
prints it to the container log on start. HTTP clients use Basic auth: the
username is always `opencode`, and only the password can be changed.

## HTTP API (agents)

Start the server explicitly (see
[Usage](usage.md#start-the-server-web-ui-http-api)), then an external agent
creates a session and sends prompts through the REST API:

```bash
BASE=http://localhost:4096
AUTH="opencode:a-long-secret"

# Server info (also a good health check)
curl -fsS -u "$AUTH" "$BASE/api/info"

# Create a session
SESSION=$(curl -fsS -u "$AUTH" -X POST "$BASE/api/session" | jq -r .id)

# Send a prompt
curl -fsS -u "$AUTH" -X POST "$BASE/api/session/$SESSION/prompt" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"parts": [{"type": "text", "text": "Summarize this repository"}]}'

# Subscribe to server events
curl -fsS -u "$AUTH" -N "$BASE/api/event"
```

- The OpenAPI 3.1 document of a running server is served at
  `http://localhost:4096/openapi.json`; the published reference lives at
  <https://opencode.ai/docs/openapi.json>.
- The generated TypeScript client is `@opencode/client` (Promise-based
  resource clients and async iterables for streaming endpoints).
- Permission requests: the baked configuration allows `edit`, `shell` and
  `webfetch` autonomously; for `ask` outcomes, clients reply through
  `POST /api/session/{sessionID}/permission/{requestID}/reply`
  (`once`, `always`, `reject`).
- See <https://opencode.ai/docs/api> for the full endpoint reference.

## Pairing from the server side

`POST /api/pair` creates a pairing code and `GET /auth/connect/{code}`
redeems it; the `opencode pair` command wraps this flow.

# Architecture

Repository layout, the image, and the GitHub Actions pipeline.

## Layout

```text
.
├── AGENTS.md                         # instructions for agents working on this repository
├── bin/opencode-py                   # launcher: thin wrapper over podman/docker
├── Containerfile                     # OpenCode + Python/OR-Tools toolchain, built-in non-root user (uid 1000)
├── .env.example                      # runtime env template (copied into the image)
├── versions.json                     # pinned versions (updated by the bot PR)
├── .github/workflows/build.yml       # multi-arch build, publish, smoke test, pin updates
├── scripts/
│   ├── resolve-versions.sh           # resolves OpenCode, OR-Tools, Python and yq
│   └── smoke-ortools.py              # CP-SAT smoke test run by CI
├── config/
│   ├── bin/entrypoint.sh             # git identity, forge credentials, uv cache, cd into the project, exec "$@"
│   ├── gitconfig                     # generic gitconfig for the non-root user
│   ├── sudoers.d/opencode            # passwordless sudo policy (any user in the container)
│   └── opencode/                     # copied to /home/opencode/.config/opencode
│       ├── opencode.jsonc            # permissions, LSP (no model or provider pinned)
│       ├── AGENTS.md                 # agent instructions (public, no personal data)
│       └── skills/env-setup/SKILL.md # offers the env template when runtime variables are missing
├── k8s/
│   ├── deployment.yaml
│   ├── service.yaml
│   └── secret.example.yaml
├── docs/                             # detailed documentation
└── README.md
```

## Why Debian and not Alpine

The image is based on `python:<version>-slim` (Debian trixie) rather than on the
upstream Alpine OpenCode image. OR-Tools publishes `manylinux` wheels only, with
no musllinux wheel and no source distribution:

| Package                      | musllinux arm64  | manylinux arm64 |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------- | --------------- |
| numpy, pandas, scipy         | yes              | yes             |
| pyarrow, lxml, pydantic-core | yes              | yes             |
| scikit-learn, torch          | no               | yes             |
| opencv-python                | no               | yes             |
| matplotlib                   | no (aarch64)     | yes             |
| **ortools**                  | **no, no sdist** | yes             |

That is also why the Python minor follows OR-Tools: there is no fallback build
path.

## Image

The `Containerfile` starts from `python:${PYTHON_VERSION}-slim`, installs the
official OpenCode release asset for the target architecture (checksum-verified,
`opencode` and `opencode2`), the upstream `yq` binary, the Debian toolchain, and
the `uv`-managed development tools. It creates a non-root `opencode` user
(uid/gid 1000 by default, overridable with `--build-arg UID=... --build-arg
GID=...`). The documented run commands make the image's user the caller's:
Podman maps it onto the host user with
`--userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000`, Docker overrides it with `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"`,
so files created by the agent keep host ownership either way. The home and the
uv tool directories are world-writable inside the image so that any user the
container runs as can write to them (the container is a single-user trust
boundary).

The image bakes configuration, not secrets:

- `config/opencode/` → `/home/opencode/.config/opencode/` (autonomous
  permissions, the two Python language servers, the `env-setup` skill, the
  `AGENTS.md` policy; no model or provider is pinned — the session runs on
  OpenCode's free built-in models until the user connects OpenRouter);
- `config/gitconfig` → `/home/opencode/.gitconfig` (generic identity);
- `.env.example` → `/home/opencode/.env.example` (the runtime env template);
- `config/bin/entrypoint.sh` → `/usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh` (git identity
  from the environment, forge git credentials from `GH_TOKEN`, `GITLAB_TOKEN`,
  `FORGEJO_TOKEN` when set, the uv cache on the state volume, a `cd` into the
  single mounted project, then `exec "$@"`).

The default command is the interactive TUI: `docker run -it ... image` opens a
session with no OpenCode installation on the host, in the mounted project (the
entrypoint `cd`s into it when it is the only project mount). The server
(`opencode serve --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 4096`) is started explicitly — the
k8s deployment and the CI smoke test pass it as the container command. See
[Usage](usage.md) and [Access](api.md).

## CI pipeline

`.github/workflows/build.yml` runs on push to `main`, on a daily schedule, and
on demand (`workflow_dispatch`):

1. **resolve** — `scripts/resolve-versions.sh` resolves the newest stable
   OpenCode release, the newest OR-Tools release, the newest yq release, and the
   CPython minor that OR-Tools supports, then the newest
   `python:3.<minor>.<patch>-slim` tag for it.
2. **build** — a matrix on native runners (`ubuntu-26.04` for amd64,
   `ubuntu-26.04-arm` for arm64) builds and pushes each architecture by digest,
   with a per-architecture registry cache. Each job pulls its own digest and
   runs the smoke test natively: the default `CMD` must be the TUI, the toolchain
   must answer, OR-Tools must install and solve a CP-SAT model, and the server
   must answer `GET /api/info` with Basic auth and report the built version.
3. **merge** — `docker buildx imagetools create` assembles the digests into the
   multi-arch tags `latest`, `oc-<opencode>-py<python>` and `<YYYYMMDD>`.
4. **update-pins** — compares the resolved versions with `versions.json` and
   opens a pull request (`peter-evans/create-pull-request`) when they differ.

The cache lives in a separate `opencode-python-buildcache` GHCR repository, one
tag per architecture. See [Updating](updating.md) for the version rules.

# Installation

How to open the first session. There is nothing to install: the image is
pulled automatically on the first run, and the TUI runs inside the container,
so no OpenCode client is needed on the host.

## Requirements

- [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) or [rootless Podman](https://podman.io/).
  For Podman, enable subuid mappings so the
  `--userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000` flag works (`subuid`/`subgid` entries
  in `/etc/subuid` and `/etc/subgid`).
- Nothing else: OpenCode's free built-in models work without any account or
  key. An [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/) API key is optional — see
  [More models](#more-models-optional).
- On Apple Silicon the image runs natively: it is published for
  `linux/arm64` as well as `linux/amd64`, so no emulation is involved. Use a
  current Docker Desktop or Podman; see [Apple Silicon](#apple-silicon).

## Open the first session

From the project directory you want the agent to work in:

Podman:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 \
  --name "opencode-$$" \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-python-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest
```

Docker (the same, with `--user` instead of `--userns`):

```bash
docker run -it --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  --name "opencode-$$" \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-python-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest
```

`--userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000` (Podman) maps the image's built-in user
(uid 1000) onto your host user, so files the agent creates are uid 1000 in the
container and yours on the host; the Docker command passes `--user
"$(id -u):$(id -g)"` instead, running the agent as your host UID directly.

The TUI opens inside the container; the project is mounted read-write at
`/home/opencode/projects/<name>` and OpenCode starts inside it, so the session
opens your project directly. The `opencode-python-state-<user>` volume (one per
user) keeps credentials, the session database, the uv cache and any extra
Python versions across runs. The session starts on OpenCode's free built-in
model — start typing right away, no key needed; the sidebar's `/connect` hint
leads to other models (see [More models](#more-models-optional)).

## Apple Silicon

The image is a multi-arch manifest, so Docker and Podman select `linux/arm64`
on an M-series Mac automatically; do not pass `--platform`. Python wheels,
including OR-Tools, are native `manylinux` aarch64 builds — nothing runs under
Rosetta or QEMU.

- Podman on macOS runs an arm64 Linux VM (`podman machine`). Docker Desktop
  needs a recent version; an old release may pull the amd64 image and emulate
  it, which is much slower.
- Give the VM enough memory: CP-SAT is memory hungry and the language servers
  add up. 8 GB for the VM is a comfortable default, see
  [Optimization](optimization.md#resources).
- Enable virtiofs file sharing (Podman's default on current releases, Docker
  Desktop's "Virtualization framework" option). A Python virtual environment
  with OR-Tools is large, so bind-mount performance matters; see
  [Optimization](optimization.md#virtual-environments) for keeping the venv on
  the state volume instead.

## More models (optional)

The free built-in models need no key. To use OpenRouter models, connect
OpenRouter once; two ways, and when both are present, the stored account wins.

### Option 1: connect in the TUI (`/connect`)

With the TUI open, type `/connect`, pick OpenRouter, and enter the API key.
The credential is stored in your `opencode-python-state-<user>` volume, so every
later run has the models. The same credential can be stored from the host
without the TUI:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 \
  --name "opencode-$$" \
  -v opencode-python-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest opencode auth login openrouter
```

The same works with Docker (with `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` instead of
`--userns`). Remove the stored key the same way, with `opencode auth logout
openrouter` in place of `auth login openrouter`.

### Option 2: environment file

Keep the key on the host: put it in a `.env` file in the project folder — ask
the agent to create it (it copies the template from the image into the current
folder, which is on the host), or copy [.env.example](../.env.example) from the
repository — fill in `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, keep it private with `chmod 600
.env`, add it to `.gitignore`, and pass it on the run command:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 \
  --name "opencode-$$" \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-python-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  --env-file .env \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest
```

The same works with Docker (with `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` instead of
`--userns`). See [Security notes](security.md) for how secrets are handled.

Either way, the OpenRouter models then appear in the TUI's model picker — pick
the one you want to work with; the pick is remembered on the
`opencode-python-state-<user>` volume and used on later runs.

## The launcher (optional)

The repository ships `bin/opencode-py`, a thin wrapper over podman/docker for
people who prefer a shorter command: it resolves the engine (Podman first,
override with `OPENCODE_PY_ENGINE`), mounts the current project and the
`opencode-python-state-<user>` volume, finds the env file on its own
(`OPENCODE_PY_ENV_FILE` → `./.env` → `~/.config/opencode-python/env`), and
passes all remaining arguments to opencode unchanged. Fetch the single file
from the repository and install it:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/app/opencode-python/main/bin/opencode-py \
  -o /tmp/opencode-py
install -m755 /tmp/opencode-py "$HOME/.local/bin/opencode-py"
```

Then run `opencode-py` from the project directory (`opencode-py -r
../other-model` mounts a sibling read-only, `OPENCODE_PY_RUN_ARGS="--cpus 4
--memory 8g"` gives CP-SAT room to work, `OPENCODE_PY_RUN_ARGS="-p 4096:4096"`
publishes the port in server mode). It is optional: every launcher flag has a
plain `run` equivalent shown in [Usage](usage.md).

## Image tags

The image is published to GHCR by the GitHub Actions workflow. Tags:
`latest`, `oc-<opencode-version>-py<python-version>` (the exact toolchain
combination, for example `oc-2.3.2-py3.14.10`) and `<YYYYMMDD>` (build date).
See [Updating](updating.md) for how versions are chosen.

## Uninstall

Remove the image and the state volume:

```bash
podman rmi ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest
podman volume rm opencode-python-state-$(id -un)
```

# Kubernetes

Running the OpenCode server in a cluster with the example manifests in
`k8s/`.

## Prerequisites

- A Kubernetes cluster and `kubectl`.
- A pull secret for GHCR (replace the placeholders):

  ```bash
  kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-pull \
    --docker-server=https://ghcr.io \
    --docker-username=<you> \
    --docker-password=<ghcr-token>
  ```

- A runtime `Secret` based on [k8s/secret.example.yaml](../k8s/secret.example.yaml)
  with real values, applied to the target namespace.

## Deploy

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
```

The deployment pins the image's built-in user (uid/gid 1000): the image
default is the interactive TUI, so the manifest passes the server command
explicitly in the container `args`. It keeps credentials, the session
database and the uv cache on the `opencode-state` PVC and mounts an `emptyDir`
as the agent working space. It uses `Recreate` because a single writer owns
the state volume.

The image is a multi-arch manifest, so the same deployment works on amd64 and
arm64 nodes; no `nodeSelector` or `--platform` is needed.

The Service exposes port 4096 as `ClusterIP` by default; switch `type` to
`LoadBalancer` for external access.

## Access

```bash
kubectl port-forward svc/opencode 4096:4096
```

Then use the HTTP API as described in [Access](api.md#http-api-agents) with
`http://localhost:4096` and your `OPENCODE_PASSWORD`.

## Notes

- Probes are TCP, because the HTTP API requires Basic auth and probes cannot
  send credentials.
- The `emptyDir` project volume is wiped when the pod restarts. Replace it
  with a `PersistentVolumeClaim` or a projected volume when the project must
  persist.
- Solver runs need memory and CPU: raise the container resources beyond the
  example values for real optimization workloads (see
  [Optimization](optimization.md#resources)).
- Update the `image` field (or pin the `oc-<version>-py<python>` tag instead of
  `latest`) when you move to a new release; see [Updating](updating.md).
- Secrets in the `Secret` are visible to the pod; treat the pod as trusted
  for them, as documented in [Security notes](security.md).

# Optimization

The image is built for Python developers who work on optimization with Google
OR-Tools. This page covers what is guaranteed, how to start a project, how to
size the container, and what to do when a solver run needs more.

## What is guaranteed

- OR-Tools is **not** baked into the image; it is a project dependency, so each
  project pins its own version. The image guarantees a compatible runtime and
  verifies it in CI.
- The base is Debian/glibc with native wheels for both architectures. OR-Tools
  publishes `manylinux_2_28` wheels for CPython 3.9 and newer on `x86_64` and
  `aarch64`, and publishes **no musllinux wheel and no source distribution**, so
  an Alpine image could not install it at all.
- The Python minor is chosen from the OR-Tools release: `resolve-versions.sh`
  reads the `cp3XY` wheel tags of the newest `ortools` and builds the image on
  the newest `python:3.X.Y-slim` for that minor. Today that is CPython 3.14 and
  OR-Tools 9.15.
- The CI smoke test installs OR-Tools in a throwaway environment and solves a
  small CP-SAT model on `linux/amd64` **and** `linux/arm64`, which is exactly
  what Apple Silicon users get.

## Quick start

```bash
cd /home/opencode/projects/<your-project>
uv init
uv add ortools
uv run python - <<'PY'
from ortools.sat.python import cp_model

model = cp_model.CpModel()
x = model.NewIntVar(0, 10, "x")
y = model.NewIntVar(0, 10, "y")
model.Add(x + 2 * y <= 14)
model.Maximize(3 * x + 2 * y)

solver = cp_model.CpSolver()
solver.parameters.num_search_workers = 4
print(solver.Solve(model), solver.Value(x), solver.Value(y))
PY
```

A CP-SAT model over real data usually wants `pandas` (and `matplotlib` for
plots); add them the same way:

```bash
uv add pandas matplotlib
```

## Solvers

| Solver      | Package                | Notes                                                  |
| ----------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| CP-SAT      | `ortools`              | constraint programming / MIP, the main OR-Tools solver |
| GLOP        | `ortools`              | linear programming                                     |
| SCIP        | `ortools` (`pywraplp`) | mixed-integer programming, bundled with OR-Tools       |
| HiGHS       | `highspy`              | fast open-source LP/MIP, separate package              |
| PuLP, Pyomo | `pulp`, `pyomo`        | modeling layers over the solvers above                 |

All of these install from wheels on both architectures. Commercial solvers
(Gurobi, CPLEX) are not part of the image; they need their own licences and are
installed per project if you have them.

## Resources

CP-SAT uses all visible cores by default and keeps a search tree in memory.
Give the container room:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --cpus 4 --memory 8g \
  --name "opencode-$$" \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-python-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest
```

- Cap the search with `solver.parameters.num_search_workers = N` when the
  container has fewer CPUs than the host.
- `solver.parameters.max_time_in_seconds` keeps exploratory runs bounded.
- Docker Desktop and Podman machine default to a small VM; raise the VM memory
  (8 GB is a comfortable default) rather than only the container limit.
- With the [launcher](installation.md#the-launcher-optional), the same is
  `OPENCODE_PY_RUN_ARGS="--cpus 4 --memory 8g" opencode-py`.

## Virtual environments

`uv` creates `.venv` in the project by default. A virtual environment with
OR-Tools is roughly 300 MB across thousands of files, which is slow on the
bind mount of a macOS VM. On Apple Silicon, keep it on the state volume
instead:

```bash
export UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/home/opencode/.local/share/venv
```

The environment then lives next to the uv cache and survives container
restarts. The trade-off is that host-side tooling cannot reuse it (`.pinned`
and the lockfile in the project still define it).

## Profiling

`py-spy` profiles native frames, including OR-Tools solver calls, without
changing the code:

```bash
py-spy top -- uv run python model.py
py-spy record -o profile.svg -- uv run python model.py
```

## Notes

- OR-Tools pins `protobuf<6.34`; do not force a newer protobuf alongside it.
- Solver output goes to stdout/stderr inside the container; keep
  `num_search_workers` reasonable when running in server mode so the TUI stays
  responsive.
- Kernels and notebooks are not baked in. Add `jupyterlab` to the project
  (`uv add jupyterlab`, then `uv run jupyter lab --ip=0.0.0.0 --no-browser`) if
  you want them; publishing the port works the same way as the server mode in
  [Usage](usage.md).

# Security notes

## Trust model

- OpenCode never runs as root: in every documented mode it is the image's
  built-in user, uid/gid 1000 (Podman maps it onto your host user with
  `--userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000`; Docker runs it as your host UID with
  `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"`; the k8s manifest pins `runAsUser: 1000`).
  That user has passwordless sudo; the policy is broad by design
  (`NOPASSWD: ALL`) and constrained by the usage rules in the baked
  `AGENTS.md`. The home and uv tool directories are world-writable inside the
  image so any `--user` can write to them. Container root maps to a subuid on
  the host (rootless Podman) or to root in the pod (Kubernetes). Treat the
  container as the security boundary: the agent can effectively do anything the
  container can.
- The baked permissions allow the agent to `edit` files, run `shell` commands,
  and `webfetch` URLs without prompts, so it works autonomously. Only mount
  projects and tokens the agent is allowed to touch.
- The container runs the agent, not your desktop: do not mount sensitive host
  directories (SSH agent, cloud credentials) unless the task needs them.
- Solver licences are not in the image. If you add a commercial solver to a
  project, its licence file becomes part of that project and is as sensitive as
  any other credential.

## Secrets

- Secrets live only on the host or on the state volume: the runtime env file
  (`chmod 600`), the calling environment, a Kubernetes `Secret`, or a connected
  account (`opencode auth login`). Nothing secret is baked into the image; the
  image ships the documented template (`/home/opencode/.env.example`) instead.
- Every process in the container, including the agent, sees the forwarded
  variables. A forge token (`GH_TOKEN`, `GITLAB_TOKEN`, `FORGEJO_TOKEN`) is
  usable by the agent for anything that token can do — prefer a dedicated token
  with the minimum scopes.
- `UV_INDEX_URL` may embed credentials for a private package index. Prefer a
  read-only token, and remember that the agent can read it from its environment.
- The `OPENCODE_PASSWORD` (or the generated one printed to the log) protects
  the HTTP API with Basic auth in server mode. Keep the log private when the
  password is generated.
- The state volume (`/home/opencode/.local`) holds provider credentials, the
  session database, the uv cache and any extra Python interpreters; treat it as
  sensitive.
- Never commit a `.env` file. The `env-setup` skill offers to copy the template
  into the working folder when runtime variables are missing, keeps the agent
  from writing secrets into the repository and reminds about `chmod 600`.

## Network

- In server mode the server listens on `0.0.0.0` inside the container. Expose
  the port only to the networks that need it (host port, `ClusterIP` service,
  or a `LoadBalancer` with authentication in front). The default TUI mode does
  not listen on any port.
- Pairing links are single-use and expire in 5 minutes; web sessions last
  30 days and are revoked when the password changes.
- `uv` and the language servers reach the package index and the model provider
  from inside the container; there is no separate egress control. On a
  restricted network, point `UV_INDEX_URL` at an internal mirror.

# Toolchain

The image is built for Python agent work with an optimization focus: Python,
`uv`, the lint/type/test tools, the language servers, and the C toolchain for
building extensions.

| Area      | Tools                                                                                                      |
| --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Python    | CPython (`python`, `python3`, `python3.14`), `uv`                                                          |
| Quality   | `ruff` (lint and format), `basedpyright`, `mypy`, `pytest`, `pre-commit`                                   |
| Profiling | `py-spy`                                                                                                   |
| Search    | `rg` (ripgrep), `fd`, `ast-grep` (`sg`)                                                                    |
| Data      | `jq`, `yq`                                                                                                 |
| Git       | `git`, `openssh-client`, `gh`, `glab`                                                                      |
| Build     | `gcc`/`g++`, `make`, `pkg-config`, `libssl-dev`, `libffi-dev`, `zlib1g-dev`, `libsqlite3-dev`              |
| Shell     | `bash`, `shellcheck`, `shfmt`, GNU userland (`coreutils`, `findutils`, `grep`, `sed`, `gawk`, `diffutils`) |
| Misc      | `less`, `file`, `tree`, `curl`, `xz`, `unzip`, `zip`, `tzdata`, `procps`                                   |

The base is Debian (`python:<version>-slim`), not Alpine, because OR-Tools and
most of the numerical Python ecosystem publish `manylinux` wheels only — see
[Optimization](optimization.md).

## Python

The image is built on the official `python:<version>-slim` image, so the
interpreter is the Debian-friendly upstream CPython build at `/usr/local`, and
`python`, `python3` and `python3.14` point at it:

```bash
python -V                    # the CPython pinned at build time
uv --version
```

The pinned version is the newest CPython that OR-Tools ships wheels for
(recorded in `versions.json` and in the image labels). A project that needs
another version declares it in `.python-version` (or `requires-python`, which
`uv` honors); `uv` downloads that interpreter into the state volume on demand:

```bash
uv python install 3.12
uv venv --python 3.12
```

## uv

`uv` is installed from PyPI at build time (Debian trixie does not package it).
It owns environments and packages; do not install into the system interpreter:

```bash
uv init
uv add ortools highspy pandas matplotlib
uv run python model.py
uvx ruff check .
```

- `uv sync` / `uv add` use `.venv` in the project by default. See
  [Optimization](optimization.md#virtual-environments) for the macOS-friendly
  alternative.
- The uv cache is redirected to `$HOME/.local/share/uv-cache` by the
  entrypoint, which sits on the state volume, so large wheels such as OR-Tools
  are not downloaded again on every run.
- `uv tool install <tool>` adds a tool for the current user under
  `$HOME/.local` (also on the state volume) and puts it first on the `PATH`.
  `uv tool list` shows those user-installed tools; the baked tools are in
  `/opt/uv/tools` and their executables in `/opt/uv/bin`.

## Lint, types, tests

`ruff`, `basedpyright`, `mypy`, `pytest`, `pre-commit` and `py-spy` are
installed as isolated `uv tool` environments at build time, with their
executables in `/opt/uv/bin` (on the `PATH`), so they run without a project
environment:

```bash
ruff check .
ruff format .
mypy src/
pytest
py-spy record -o profile.svg -- python model.py
```

The language servers are wired into OpenCode through the baked configuration:
`basedpyright-langserver --stdio` for types and navigation, and `ruff server`
for lint and format diagnostics, both covering `.py` and `.pyi`.

## Installing extra packages

The user the container runs as has passwordless sudo (the policy matches any
user), so the agent can install Debian packages when a task needs them:

```bash
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends <package>
```

Runtime installs are not persisted: they disappear with the container. Add the
package to the `Containerfile` for a permanent tool. The usage policy is
defined in the baked `AGENTS.md`; see [Security notes](security.md).

## Building C extensions

`gcc`/`g++`, `make`, `pkg-config` and the common development headers are
installed, so source builds of Python packages work when no wheel exists. Build
dependencies that a specific package needs (for example database client
libraries) can be added with apt for the session; for a permanent one, add
them to the `Containerfile`.

# Troubleshooting

Common errors and fixes.

## The TUI does not start or looks broken

- The TUI needs an interactive terminal: run the container with `-it`.
  Without a TTY the TUI cannot start.
- No colors or a garbled screen: `TERM` is inherited from the calling
  environment, so make sure it is set on the host (for example
  `xterm-256color`).
- The TUI talks to the local process inside the container and needs no
  password; if a provider error appears, check the OpenRouter key (below).
- The default command is the TUI; if the container starts a server instead,
  either a custom command was passed (for example by the k8s manifest) or the
  local image is stale. `podman run` and `docker run` reuse a local image
  without re-pulling it: run
  `podman pull ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest` and start again.
- The TUI opens at `/home/opencode/projects` instead of your project: that
  is expected when several projects are mounted (or none). Open a specific
  project by appending its directory to the run command:
  `opencode /home/opencode/projects/<name>`.
- `ctrl-p` (the command palette) does nothing: your run command lacks
  `--detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q"`. The default detach sequence of
  podman/docker is `ctrl-p ctrl-q`, so the engine waits for `ctrl-q` and
  the key never reaches the TUI. Every command in this repository carries
  the flag; alternatively set `detachKeys` in your engine's client config
  file.

## The server does not respond (server mode)

- Server mode is an explicit command: the container must be started with
  `opencode serve --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 4096` (the k8s manifest and the
  CI smoke test do this; the image default is the TUI).
- Check the container is running and the port is published:
  `podman ps` / `docker ps`, and the `-p 4096:4096` flag.
- The server binds `0.0.0.0:4096` inside the container; without the port
  publication the host cannot reach it.
- Give it a few seconds on first start, then check the log for the
  `server listening on http://0.0.0.0:4096` line: find the container name in
  [Usage](usage.md#logs), then `podman logs -f <name>`.
- In Kubernetes, the pod must be `Ready` (TCP probe) and the Service must
  select `app: opencode`; `kubectl port-forward svc/opencode 4096:4096`.

## Authentication errors (HTTP 401, server mode)

- The username is always `opencode`; only the password changes.
- When `OPENCODE_PASSWORD` is empty, the server generated a password and
  printed it to the container log on start (find the name in
  [Usage](usage.md#logs), then `podman logs -f <name>`; in Kubernetes:
  `kubectl logs deploy/opencode`).
- Pairing links for the web UI do not use the password at all; the browser
  session is created through the one-time link.

## No model or provider errors

- A 401/"missing API key" from OpenRouter means the container has no OpenRouter
  key: neither `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` in the environment nor a connected
  account. Connect once in the TUI with `/connect` (the key is stored on
  your `opencode-python-state-<user>` volume), or set the variable in the env
  file (or the Kubernetes Secret) and restart with `--env-file` / the updated
  Secret.
- Without any key the TUI opens on a free built-in model and the agent
  answers without a key. For more models, connect OpenRouter (see
  [Installation](installation.md#more-models-optional)).
- When the agent is running and another variable (for example a forge token)
  is missing, the `env-setup` skill offers to copy the template from
  `/home/opencode/.env.example` into the working folder.

## OR-Tools does not install or import

- Install it in the project, not globally: `uv add ortools` (`uv run python -c
"from ortools.sat.python import cp_model"` to check).
- `No matching distribution found` for `ortools` on Alpine/musl: OR-Tools has
  no musllinux wheel and no source distribution. This image is Debian-based for
  that reason; if you built your own image on Alpine, switch the base.
- A Python newer than OR-Tools supports has no wheel: stay on the image's
  interpreter or a version OR-Tools publishes wheels for. See
  [Optimization](optimization.md#what-is-guaranteed).
- `ImportError: libgomp.so.1` or a similar shared-library error means a runtime
  library is missing from a custom image; the published image installs
  `libgomp1`, `libatomic1` and `libstdc++6`.
- A protobuf conflict: OR-Tools pins `protobuf<6.34`; do not add a newer
  protobuf to the same environment.

## Python environments

- `uv sync` recreates or updates `.venv` in the project; activate nothing,
  use `uv run` or `.venv/bin/python`. Do not install into the system
  interpreter with `pip`.
- The venv or the uv cache is slow on macOS: the bind mount is the bottleneck.
  Put the environment on the state volume with
  `UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/home/opencode/.local/share/venv`; the cache is
  already redirected there by the entrypoint.
- A project requesting another Python version: `uv` downloads it on demand into
  the state volume. `uv python list` shows what is installed and available;
  `uv python install 3.12` pre-installs one.
- `command not found: ruff` (or `mypy`, `py-spy`, ...): the baked tools live in
  `/opt/uv/bin`, and user-installed ones in `$HOME/.local/bin` (on the state
  volume). `uv tool list` shows only the user-installed tools; the baked
  executables are in `/opt/uv/bin`. `uv tool install <tool>` adds one.

## Apple Silicon and arm64

- An `exec format error` or a very slow container means an amd64 image is being
  emulated on an arm64 host: update Docker Desktop or Podman and pull
  `ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest` again (the manifest is multi-arch).
- `docker image inspect --format '{{.Architecture}}'` must report `arm64`.
- File sharing performance: use virtiofs (Podman's default on current releases;
  in Docker Desktop enable "Virtualization framework"), and give the VM more
  memory when solvers run out of it.

## Git operations fail

- Git over HTTPS is preconfigured by the entrypoint from the tokens in the
  container environment: `GH_TOKEN` (GitHub, via `gh auth setup-git`),
  `GITLAB_TOKEN` (+ `GITLAB_URL`) and `FORGEJO_TOKEN` (+ `FORGEJO_URL`).
  Check that the token for the host you push to is set.
- Commits are signed with the `GIT_AUTHOR_*` / `GIT_COMMITTER_*` variables or
  the baked generic identity; set the variables in the env file.
- Permission denied on files in the project (the agent cannot create, edit
  or commit): the run command must carry the user mapping —
  `--userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000` (Podman) or `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"`
  (Docker), so files it writes are owned by your host user (every command in
  [Usage](usage.md) includes it).

## The image looks stale

- Pull the tag you expect: `docker pull ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest` and
  compare the labels with the current pins in `versions.json`:
  `docker image inspect --format '{{json .Config.Labels}}' <image>`.
- To force a new build without waiting for the schedule, run the `Build`
  workflow from the repository's Actions page.

# Updating

How versions are chosen and how image releases work.

## Rolling latest

The image always builds with the current upstream versions — there is nothing
to update on the host:

- **OpenCode**: the newest non-prerelease release tag of `anomalyco/opencode`
  from the GitHub releases API.
- **OR-Tools**: the newest release on PyPI.
- **Python**: the newest `python:3.<minor>.<patch>-slim` tag on Docker Hub for
  the newest CPython minor that has an OR-Tools wheel (free-threaded `cp3XYt`
  wheels are ignored). This bound matters: OR-Tools ships no source
  distribution, so a Python new enough to have no wheel cannot be used.
- **yq**: the newest mikefarah/yq release, downloaded from GitHub for the target
  architecture.
- **uv and the Debian packages** (`ruff` comes from `uv tool`, `gh`, `glab`,
  `ripgrep`, ...) are whatever the distribution or PyPI publishes on build day.
  Debian trixie does not package `uv`, so the image installs the current `uv`
  from PyPI during the build.

The workflow resolves them on every run (push to `main`, the daily schedule at
06:17 UTC, or `workflow_dispatch`) and rebuilds the image. The scheduled run is
also the version watch: it always rebuilds with whatever upstream published, and
the final job compares the resolved versions with `versions.json`, opening the
pin update pull request only when something moved.

## The last-build badge

The README's second badge shows the date, time and versions of the last build.
The `status` job runs at the end of every `main` build (successful or not) and
force-pushes a single-file branch, `status`, whose `status.json` follows the
[shields.io endpoint](https://shields.io/badges/endpoint-badge) schema. The
branch is written by CI only; do not edit it by hand.

## Image tags

| Tag                                        | Meaning                                |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| `latest`                                   | the newest published build, multi-arch |
| `oc-<opencode-version>-py<python-version>` | the exact combination, for pinning     |
| `<YYYYMMDD>`                               | the build date                         |

Run the version that was current when you read the docs, or pin:

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:oc-2.3.2-py3.14.10
```

`docker image inspect` prints the pinned versions from the image labels
(`org.opencode-python.opencode`, `org.opencode-python.python`,
`org.opencode-python.yq`).

## Pin updates in the repository

`versions.json` records the last resolved combination (OpenCode, OR-Tools,
Python, yq). The `update-pins` job opens a pull request (branch
`chore/update-pinned-versions`) whenever the resolved versions differ from the
file. Merging the PR rebuilds and republishes the image; the schedule keeps
looking for newer versions on its own.

## Building locally

For a one-off build with specific upstream versions (both architectures need a
matching builder; the CI matrix uses native runners):

```bash
docker build \
  --build-arg OPENCODE_VERSION=2.3.2 \
  --build-arg PYTHON_VERSION=3.14.10 \
  --build-arg YQ_VERSION=4.54.3 \
  -t opencode-python:local .
```

The `Containerfile` never hardcodes versions, so the workflow remains the
source of truth.

# Usage

Running the container: the TUI, the server mode, mounts, resources, secrets and
other commands.

## Open the TUI (default)

The default command is the interactive TUI inside the container. From the
project directory:

Podman:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 \
  --name "opencode-$$" \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-python-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest
```

Docker (the same, with `--user` instead of `--userns`):

```bash
docker run -it --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  --name "opencode-$$" \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-python-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest
```

No server, no published port, and nothing installed on the host. The project
directory is mounted read-write at `/home/opencode/projects/<name>`; when it
is the only project mount, OpenCode starts inside it, so the TUI opens your
project directly. If you have a `.env` file (see
[More models](installation.md#more-models-optional)), add `--env-file .env`
to the command. The optional
[launcher](installation.md#the-launcher-optional) wraps exactly this.

## Start the server (web UI, HTTP API)

Server mode is an explicit command on top of the same image:

```bash
podman run -d \
  --name "opencode-$$" \
  --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 -p 4096:4096 \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  -v opencode-python-state-$(id -un):/home/opencode/.local \
  --env-file .env \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest \
  opencode serve --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 4096
```

The same works with Docker (with `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` instead of
`--userns`); drop `-d` and add `-it` for a foreground run. The
[launcher](installation.md#the-launcher-optional) equivalent is
`OPENCODE_PY_RUN_ARGS="-p 4096:4096" opencode-py serve --hostname 0.0.0.0
--port 4096`.

To open the [web UI](api.md#web-ui), create a pairing link from inside the
running container:
`podman exec -it --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" <name> opencode pair`
(`<name>` is the container name, see [Logs](#logs)), and open the printed
link in a browser. The [HTTP API](api.md#http-api-agents) is available under
Basic auth on the same port.

## Mounts

| Host path                             | Container path                   | Purpose                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| your project directory                | `/home/opencode/projects/<name>` | the agent's working project; OpenCode starts inside it when it is the only mount |
| `opencode-python-state-<user>` volume | `/home/opencode/.local`          | credentials, the session database, the uv cache and extra Pythons, per user      |

- User mapping: `--userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000` (Podman) runs the agent
  as the image's built-in user, uid/gid 1000, mapped onto your host user, so
  files it creates — in the project and on the state volume — are uid 1000 in
  the container and yours on the host. Docker has no user mapping, so its
  commands pass `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` instead, which runs the agent as
  your host UID with the same ownership outcome.
- `--detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q"` (in every command above) moves the
  engine's detach sequence off the default `ctrl-p ctrl-q`, which would
  swallow the TUI's `ctrl-p` command palette key.
- `--name "opencode-$$"` (in every command in this repository) names the
  container after the PID of the shell that ran it, so parallel sessions in
  different terminals do not collide and `podman ps` stays readable.
- Mount sibling projects read-only with extra `-v` mounts under
  `/home/opencode/projects/`, for example
  `-v ../other-model:/home/opencode/projects/other-model:ro` (the launcher's
  `-r` flag wraps this). With several project mounts, OpenCode starts at
  the projects root; open a specific one by appending its directory to the
  run command: `opencode /home/opencode/projects/other-model`.
- For Kubernetes, see [Kubernetes](kubernetes.md) instead.

## Resources

Solver runs are CPU- and memory-hungry, and the language servers plus the TUI
need headroom. Pass engine limits on the run command (or through
`OPENCODE_PY_RUN_ARGS` with the launcher):

```bash
podman run -it --rm --cpus 4 --memory 8g ...
```

CP-SAT uses all apparent cores by default; set
`solver.parameters.num_search_workers` in the model when you want to cap it.
See [Optimization](optimization.md) for solver-specific advice.

## Passing secrets

Secrets are never baked into the image; they are passed at runtime:

```bash
--env-file path/to/env            # one NAME=value per line
-e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...         # or individual variables
```

The OpenRouter key is optional (the free built-in models need no key); to
connect, use the TUI's `/connect` command (see
[Installation](installation.md#more-models-optional)) — the stored account
wins over the environment.

By convention the file lives in the project directory (`.env`); the optional
[launcher](installation.md#the-launcher-optional) finds it on its own. The
template documenting every variable lives in the repository root
(`.env.example`) and inside the image at `/home/opencode/.env.example`.
Variable reference:

| Variable                                     | Required         | Purpose                                                              |
| -------------------------------------------- | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`                         | no               | API key for OpenRouter models; the free built-in models need no key  |
| `OPENCODE_PASSWORD`                          | no (server mode) | server password; when empty, one is generated and printed to the log |
| `GH_TOKEN`                                   | no               | GitHub token for git over HTTPS and the `gh` CLI                     |
| `GITLAB_TOKEN`                               | no               | GitLab token for git, the `glab` CLI and the API                     |
| `GITLAB_URL`                                 | no               | self-hosted GitLab host (default `https://gitlab.com`)               |
| `FORGEJO_URL`                                | no               | Forgejo/Gitea instance URL, required for `FORGEJO_TOKEN`             |
| `FORGEJO_TOKEN`                              | no               | Forgejo token for git and the REST API                               |
| `UV_INDEX_URL`                               | no               | private Python package index for `uv` (token may be in the URL)      |
| `GIT_AUTHOR_NAME` / `GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL`       | no               | author identity for commits                                          |
| `GIT_COMMITTER_NAME` / `GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL` | no               | committer identity for commits                                       |

When the agent is already running and a token or another variable is missing,
it can offer to copy the template into the working folder (the `env-setup`
skill). Never commit or print secrets; see [Security notes](security.md).

## Other commands

The entrypoint execs the command you pass, so any other opencode command or a
shell works — append it to the run command:

```bash
podman run -it --rm --userns=keep-id:uid=1000,gid=1000 \
  --name "opencode-$$" \
  -v "$PWD:/home/opencode/projects/$(basename "$PWD")" \
  --detach-keys="ctrl-],ctrl-q" \
  ghcr.io/app/opencode-python:latest \
  opencode run "Explain this repository"
```

That is a one-shot prompt with no server. For a shell inside the container,
replace the command with `bash`; `uv`, `ruff` and the rest are on the `PATH`.

## Logs

The container name (and its published ports) is shown by:

```bash
podman ps --format "table {{.ID}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Names}}\t{{.Ports}}" | grep opencode
```

The log is read with `podman logs -f <name>`. In server mode, the generated
server password (when `OPENCODE_PASSWORD` is empty) is printed there on start.
